s: Mein Busen fängt mir an zu brennen! Entfernen wir uns nur geschwind!
I feel a burning starting in my breast! Let us be off posthaste!
Sag mir, wo die Blumen sind / Mädchen pflückten sie geschwind
Tell me, where the flowers are / Girls have picked them swiftly
geschwind.et: From Middle High German swinde, from Old High German *swind, from Proto-West Germanic *swinþ. See English swith.

s: Auf deutschen Autobahnen gibt es keine allgemeine Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung.
On German motorways, there is no general speed limit.
Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung.et: From Geschwindigkeit (“speed, pace, velocity”) + -s- + Begrenzung (“limit, demarcation”).

s: Man kann den Zug nicht verlangsamen, geschweige denn anhalten.
You can't slow down the train, let alone stop it.
let alone; used after a negative or limiting clause to introduce another that applies even less
let alone; used after an affirmative clause to introduce another that applies even more
geschweige.et: First-person singular indicative present of geschweigen (“to be silent”) (from Middle High German geswîgen, from Old High German giswîgên), which has been obsolete at least since the 18th century.

Geschwür.et: From Middle High German geswër (“abscess”). Related to Russian хворь.

Geschwister.et: From Middle High German geswister, from Old High German giswëstar, equivalent to ge- + Schwester. Compare Old Saxon gisustrōni (“sibling”), Old Frisian swesterne, susterne, sisterne (“siblings”), Old English ġesweostren (“maternal cousin, sister”).

s: nonsense, gibberish (speech or writing that is meaningless, or pointless and vague)
Dann verkünden viele Abgeordnete mit Gemurre im Saal, vor allem aber mit Tweets ihr Entsetzen. Von „sinnfreiem Geschwafel“ schreibt zum Beispiel der Linke Niklas Schrader.

Geschwulst.et: From Middle High German geswulst, from Old High German giswulst, from the root of Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).

s: faggotry; gayness; behaviour associated with that of male homosexuals, such as lack of valour
Geschwuchtel.et: Derived from ge- + Schwuchtel (“faggot, fruit, poof”), as if through a verb * schwuchteln (“to behave like a faggot”).

s: a formation, now equivalent to a wing (RAF) or group (USAF), in earlier use (WWI) to a squadron
a group of animals, chiefly birds
Geschwader.et: 16th century, from ge- (collective prefix) + Schwader. The latter is from Middle High German swader, from Italian squadra. The sense “group of birds” (16th century and thus predating aviation) is derived from the cavalry use.

s: sibling (usually restricted to children and not used of adults)
child of a sibling, niece, nephew, or (in the plural, reciprocally) first cousins

Geschwist.et: Back-formation from Geschwister n pl, in which -er is part of the stem, but is reinterpreted here as a plural ending.

s: strong genitive/dative singular of geschweifte Klammer
strong genitive plural of geschweifte Klammer
inflection of geschweifte Klammer: strong dative plural
inflection of geschweifte Klammer: weak/mixed nominative/genitive/dative/accusative plural

Geschwirr.et:
From Middle High German *geswërre, from Old High German giswerri (“swirling, buzzing”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarrī, from Proto-Germanic *swarriją, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum, whistle, sound, speak”).
Alternatively, derived from schwir…
